newsitem.title: HUNGARY: ANTENNA HUNGARIA SELLS HUF 1.5 BLN OF RECEIVABLES.
newsitem.headline: ANTENNA HUNGARIA SELLS HUF 1.5 BLN OF RECEIVABLES.

text.p: Hungary's national transmitting company Antenna Hungaria Rt has put on sale 1.5 billion forints of its outstanding receivables from Hungarian Television and Hungarian Radio.

The sale of the debts, part of almost 2.5 billion forints in unpaid broadcasting fees, will start after January 20, Antenna Hungaria spokesman Andras Ory told Hungarian economic news agency MTI-Econews on Monday.
"The total receivables of close to 2.5 billion forints are now jeopardising the operations of Antenna Hungaria," Ory said.
The company will sell debts of one billion forints out of 1.7 billion forints owed by Hungarian Radio and 500 million of the 730 million forints owed by Hungarian Television, Ory said.
Antenna has tried unsuccessfully to recover the debts through the courts, he added.
Attila Magyar, managing director Adossag Borze Kft, which is handling the sale, told Reuters there will be a threshold below which Ahntenna will not accept bids but that this has not yet been fixed.
"Antenna Hungarian will set a lower limit on the price after January 20," he said.

Antenna Hungaria's EGM at the end of January is expected to approve a 2.5 billion forint capital increase approved in December by the state privatisation agency APV, which holds a majority stake in the company.

The fresh capital is needed to enable Antenna, which transmits all of Hungary's national television and radio programmes, to prepare the country's broadcasting infrastructure for the privatisation of two national television channels and a number of radio stations later this year.
The media law passed a year ago obliges the company to establish seven new national broadcasting networks by September 1997.
The cost of the upgrade is estimated at 12 billion forints and Antenna Hungaria invited tenders last month for the provision and installation of new equipment worth 4.5 billion forints.
Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn last month discounted privatisation as a means of raising the necessary capital when he said the government had no plans to privatise the company.
"Privatising Antenna Hungaria is not on the government's agenda," Horn told reporters.
Analysts say that in practical terms the question is unlikely to be raised again until the 10-year concessions for the channels are awarded late in 1997.
There is strong opposition within Horn's Socialist Party to allowing the physical means of broadcasting programmes as well as the channels themselves to fall into foreign ownership, they say.
